overview.title: Learning a BPE vocabulary and the SubWordTokenizer (Listing 14.7)
overview.main_topic: Turning the merge loop into a full vocabulary-learning function with ranked merge rules, and a tokenizer that applies those rules to new text
overview.central_idea: A BPE vocabulary starts with every character in the corpus and grows by one merged symbol per merge until it reaches the target size. The merges are stored with their rank. To tokenize new text, each word is split into characters and the learned merges are applied in rank order (earliest learned first) until no learned merge applies.
overview.importance: This is the complete subword tokenizer that the authors train on Moby Dick on p.418. The tokenizer RoBERTa uses is described as almost the same (p.480). It also shows that BPE has two phases: learning merges from a corpus and applying them to new text.

summary:
The authors extend the merge loop of p.416 into a **full function for computing a BPE vocabulary**. The vocabulary **starts with all characters found in the input text**, and **merged symbols (larger and larger subwords) are added until it reaches the desired length**. A **separate dictionary of merge rules** is also kept, **including the rank order in which they were applied**. These ranked rules are what the tokenizer uses on new text.

**Listing 14.7** has two parts:

1. `compute_sub_word_vocabulary(dataset, vocab_size)` calls `count_and_split_words`, then sums **character frequencies** weighted by word counts (`char_counts[char] += counts[word]`) and sorts them with `most_common()`. This is why the vocabulary on p.418 begins `"[UNK]", "e", "t", "a", ...`. It then builds `vocab = ["[UNK]", ...]`.
2. A `SubWordTokenizer` class with the same interface as the earlier tokenizers. Its key method, **`bpe_merge(word)`**, loops: find all adjacent symbol pairs with `re.findall(r"(?<!\S)\S+ \S+(?!\S)", word, overlapped=True)`; stop if there are none; pick `best = min(pairs, key=lambda pair: self.merges.get(pair, 1e9))`, the pair with the **lowest rank** ("we apply merge rules in 'rank' order; more frequent pairs are merged first"); stop if `best` isn't a known merge; otherwise merge it with the same lookaround regex as `merge_pair`. `split` finds words, joins their characters with spaces, applies `bpe_merge` and collects the resulting symbols. `index` and `__call__` are the same as in the other tokenizers.

**Caution:** the printed listing is **typographically corrupted**. A large block after `vocab = ["[` (the rest of the training function, the class header and `__init__`, the start of `bpe_merge`) is missing, and so are the splitting regex and the character-joining line in `split`. These notes explain the surviving lines and give a clearly labeled reconstruction. The page ends by introducing a test on the full text of Moby Dick (p.418).

paragraphs.excerpt: We can now extend this to a full function for computing a byte-pair encoding
paragraphs.what_it_says: The merging procedure becomes a full vocabulary-learning function. The vocabulary starts with all characters in the input text, and merged symbols are added until it reaches the desired length. A separate dictionary records the merge rules with the rank order in which they were applied. Next comes using these rules to tokenize new text.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Training BPE produces two things. (1) A vocabulary: all base characters plus one entry per merge, so vocab_size directly sets the number of merges (vocab_size minus the number of characters minus 1 for "[UNK]"). (2) An ordered list of merges: the recipe for segmenting any new word in the same way the training corpus was segmented.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Starting from all characters is why the tokenizer never needs "[UNK]" on its training text (p.418): any word can at worst be spelled character by character. Ranked merges make tokenization deterministic and consistent with training.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Applying merges in training order reproduces how the training procedure would have segmented that word, since BPE learned the merges greedily in that order.

terminology.meaning: The position (0, 1, 2, ...) at which a merge was learned; lower rank means learned earlier, i.e. more frequent.
The target number of vocabulary entries, which determines how many merges are learned.

concepts.name: Byte-pair encoding (BPE)
concepts.definition: A subword algorithm with a training phase (learn ranked merges from a corpus) and an encoding phase (apply them to new words in rank order).
concepts.intuition: Training writes the recipe; encoding follows it step by step.
concepts.technical: Training: vocabulary = [UNK] + characters, then greedy merges until vocab_size. Encoding: split a word into characters, repeatedly merge the present pair with the lowest rank, stop when no pair has a rank.
concepts.significance: Gives deterministic segmentation of any input with a fixed-size vocabulary.
concepts.example: With the toy merges of p.416, 'brownie' → 'brown i e'.
concepts.misconception: Encoding does not recount pair frequencies in the new text; it only uses the stored ranks.

concepts.name: Ranked merge rules
concepts.definition: A dictionary mapping a pair string such as "o w" to its rank (the order in which it was learned).
concepts.intuition: A prioritized list: try the most important shortcuts first.
concepts.technical: bpe_merge picks min(pairs, key=lambda pair: self.merges.get(pair, 1e9)); unknown pairs get rank 1e9, effectively infinity.
concepts.significance: Makes encoding match the training procedure; more frequent pairs are merged first.
concepts.example: Toy ranks: 'o w'→0, 't h'→1, 'th e'→2, 'b r'→3, ...
concepts.misconception: Merging the most frequent pair in the input word is not the same thing; rank comes from the training corpus.

concepts.name: Subword tokenization
concepts.definition: Tokenization with learned units between characters and words.
concepts.intuition: Frequent words whole, rare words in pieces.
concepts.technical: SubWordTokenizer implements it with standardize → split (words → chars → bpe_merge) → index.
concepts.significance: Achieves short sequences with no [UNK] on the training text (p.418).
concepts.example: Test line: 16 subword tokens vs. 13 words vs. 63 characters.
concepts.misconception: Subword tokenizers can still produce [UNK] for characters never seen in training.

concepts.name: Overlapping regex matches
concepts.definition: Returning every match even when matches share characters; offered by the third-party regex module via overlapped=True.
concepts.intuition: In 'b r o w n' you want b r, r o, o w and w n, not just b r and o w.
concepts.technical: Standard findall resumes after the end of each match, so adjacent pairs that share a symbol would be skipped. The book imports `regex as re` on p.408; the stdlib re module has no overlapped argument.
concepts.significance: Without it, bpe_merge could miss the lowest-ranked pair and segment words inconsistently.
concepts.example: Non-overlapping on 'f o x': ['f o'] only; overlapping: ['f o', 'o x'].
concepts.misconception: This listing doesn't run with Python's built-in re; you need the regex package.

        for char in word.split():
            char_counts[char] += counts[word]
    most_common = char_counts.most_common()

            first, second = best.split()

deeper.title: Encoding a new word with the toy merges
deeper.body:
Suppose training on the toy data of p.416 produced ranks `o w`→0, `t h`→1, `th e`→2, `b r`→3, `br ow`→4, `brow n`→5, `f o`→6, `fo x`→7, `q u`→8, `qu i`→9. Tokenize **"brownie"**:

1. `b r o w n i e`: known pairs b r (3), o w (0) → merge `o w` → `b r ow n i e`
2. known pairs: b r (3) → `br ow n i e`
3. br ow (4) → `brow n i e`
4. brow n (5) → `brown i e`
5. pairs `brown i`, `i e`: neither is a rule → stop.

Tokens: `brown`, `i`, `e`. 'brownie' never appeared in training, but it is encoded with no [UNK] and reuses the learned 'brown'. (Illustrative example, not in the book.)

deeper.title: Why overlapping matches are required
deeper.body: In `b r ow n`, a non-overlapping search for `\S+ \S+` would return `b r` and then `ow n`, skipping `r ow`. If `r ow` had the lowest rank, bpe_merge would never see it and would segment the word differently from training. `overlapped=True` (from the `regex` package the chapter imports on p.408) returns all three pairs.

deeper.title: Two phases, two costs
deeper.body: Training recounts pairs over the whole corpus once per merge, so for about 1,900 merges on Moby Dick that is slow (p.418: about a minute). Encoding only touches one word at a time and needs at most (number of characters − 1) merges per word. Production tokenizers (SentencePiece, used for the mini-GPT on p.495, or Hugging Face tokenizers) implement both in compiled code with caching.

questions.question: In bpe_merge, which pair is merged at each step?
options: The most frequent pair in the input word
The pair with the lowest rank in self.merges
A random pair from the vocabulary
questions.answer: The pair with the lowest rank in self.merges
questions.explanation: best = min(pairs, key=lambda pair: self.merges.get(pair, 1e9)). The callout says merge rules are applied in rank order. Frequency in the input word isn't used. The leftmost pair is only chosen if it has the lowest rank. Nothing is random.

questions.question: What are the two conditions under which bpe_merge stops?
questions.answer: (1) No pairs remain (the word is a single symbol); (2) the best pair is not in self.merges, meaning no learned rule applies to any present pair.
questions.explanation: The two `break` statements in the printed loop.

questions.question: Why does the vocabulary start with all characters of the training text, and what does that guarantee?
questions.answer: So any word made of those characters can be encoded, at worst one character per token. That guarantees no [UNK] on text using the training character set.
questions.explanation: p.418 confirms: the vocabulary contains every character in the source text, so the worst case is tokenizing a word into individual characters.

questions.question: Why does the pair search use overlapped=True?
questions.answer: Adjacent pairs share symbols ('b r', 'r o', 'o w'); a normal findall would skip every other pair, so the lowest-rank pair might be missed.
questions.explanation: overlapped is a feature of the third-party regex module, which the chapter imports as re on p.408.

questions.question: If the training corpus contains 60 distinct characters and vocab_size = 2,000, how many merges does compute_sub_word_vocabulary learn (assuming pairs never run out)?
questions.explanation: Each merge adds exactly one vocabulary entry on top of [UNK] and the base characters (structure per the page's description; the exact character count for Moby Dick isn't given on this page).
